newsitem.title: CUBA: New aid to be slogan-free - Cuban Catholic charity.
newsitem.headline: New aid to be slogan-free - Cuban Catholic charity.

text.p: The Roman Catholic Church charity Caritas Cubana says it is expecting more aid from Cuban Americans for Cubans affected by Hurricane Lili and this time it will ensure that it carries no slogans.

The government said on Saturday it was rejecting part of a planeload of about 30 tonnes of food sent to Caritas Cubana the previous week by donors in the United States because of slogans on the packages.

Caritas Cubana President Jose Ciro Gonzalez told reporters late on Tuesday that "in the future, we can agree with donors so that their aid does not come with slogans or labels that are provocative or perhaps offensive."

Gonzalez, who is also bishop of western Pinar del Rio province, did not give details of the slogans in the shipment of rice, beans and milk. But the Rev. Thomas Wenski, an official of the Roman Catholic diocese in Miami, which channeled the aid to Caritas, gave two examples in Havana last week: "Exile" and "Love can do everything."

Gonzalez said Wenski, now back in Miami, had been asked to make sure the next shipment was slogan-free. He did not say when it would arrive. The part of the first cargo that did not cause offense -- about 23 tonnes -- has been distributed to affected areas of Villa Clara province, Gonzalez added.
Hurricane Lili swept through central and western Cuba last month. Authorities said it destroyed about 5,000 homes and damaged crops and communications.

Caritas, a network of charities run by the Catholic Church, was established in Cuba in 1992. Over the last three years the local branch has administered about $7 million worth of aid a year as Cuba's only nongovernmental aid agency. Among its activities has been distributing insulin to diabetic children.

Gonzalez, echoing Vatican Foreign Minister Jean-Louis Tauran, who visited Cuba last month, said Caritas would like a wider social role such as training people to set up small businesses. But "all this requires time," he said.

The main problem the charity has encountered is setting up a church structure in a lay state, he added. "But the church has been gaining confidence. ... The state has seen the reality of the aid that we provide."
